author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: A 1963 novel in which a depopulated Earth's survivors play a Monopoly-like game called Bluff for ownership of vast tracts of land and each other's spouses, while alien overseers from Titan watch—Dick staging property, chance, and marriage as one continuous rigged contest.
page_summary:
After a war has left Earth sparsely populated and largely sterile, the remaining humans divide their time playing Bluff, a game in which deeds to the world's real estate—and the players' marriage partners—change hands on the turn of a card. The alien Vugs of Titan, who defeated humanity, permit the game and quietly manipulate it. Pete Garden, a compulsive player who has lost and regained his holdings and wives many times over, is drawn into a lethal contest whose stakes turn out to be the survival of the human species itself.

The novel folds Dick's recurring themes—psi powers, telepathic and precognitive duels, the blurred line between human and alien—into a scenario where reality itself becomes a level of illusion deployed 'for sinister purpose,' as PKD later put it when cataloging his own books. Ownership, luck, and intimacy are all subsumed into a game whose rules are set by a hostile intelligence, so that even leisure is a form of control.

One of the fast, invention-dense Ace novels of the early 1960s, The Game-Players of Titan is uneven but characteristic, a compact demonstration of how Dick could turn a board game into a metaphysics of manipulation.
